blocks.heading: Government in the economy
blocks.text: Government can provide services and infrastructure, regulate business activity, raise revenue and influence economic conditions. Public services may support business by improving skills, transport or health. Regulation can address harms that private decisions impose on others. Fiscal policy concerns government spending and taxation; monetary policy concerns monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates. The tools differ, and their effects depend on the situation rather than being guaranteed.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: In a policy example, a road improvement shortens Omuti Foods’ delivery route while borrowing becomes more expensive. The road can reduce delivery delays and transport expense, helping the bakery reach customers. A higher borrowing cost can make a new oven less affordable, so expansion may be postponed. Government expenditure on the road is a fiscal action; the change in credit conditions belongs to monetary policy. Calling both tools taxation would hide the different mechanisms.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the difference between a government road-building programme and a change in borrowing interest rates affecting a bakery.

Road-building expenditure is a fiscal tool, while interest-rate or credit conditions belong to monetary policy. Better roads may improve deliveries; higher borrowing costs may discourage an oven purchase. The different tools work through different mechanisms, and neither effect should be treated as guaranteed regardless of the bakery’s circumstances.
